segments.script: Who gave us the word 'tissue'? And where in the animal kingdom did tissues first evolve?
segments.video_prompt: Dramatic macro zoom into a Hydra under a compound microscope, cilia waving in slow motion. Cut to a sepia-toned portrait of Xavier Bichat in a candlelit 18th-century laboratory holding a dissection tool. Title card: 'The Origins of Histology'. Dark cinematic style.

segments.script: Marcello Malpighi (1628–1694) became the founder of histology when he first examined tissue microstructure through early microscopes. Xavier Bichat (1771–1802) identified 21 elementary tissue types without a microscope — coined the term 'tissue' — and became the Father of Histology. In 1801, Karl Mayer named the science: histology. Evolutionarily, animal tissues first appeared in Phylum Coelenterata — the first phylum at the tissue-grade of organisation. This was the evolutionary turning point that made complex organs possible.
segments.video_prompt: Animated timeline from 1628 to 1801. Portrait panels appear at each date: Malpighi (1628, microscope), Bichat (1771, scalpel), Mayer (1801, text label 'Histology'). Then evolutionary ladder animation: Amoeba → Volvox → Sycon → Hydra, with 'Tissue Grade' label glowing at Hydra. Warm amber historical tones for portraits, clean vector for ladder. Voiceover narration at 140 wpm.
